lessonRef.title: Explicit model A: traits, feelings, and motivations are shown through actions

studentTask.text: This Grade 3 lesson develops traits, feelings, and motivations are shown through actions within the unit “Story Elements: Characters, Problems, and Lessons.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's explicit model a work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
Two buckets hung on the same rope above the same well, one going down whenever the other came up.

The first bucket complained without stopping. "What a miserable arrangement," it said. "No matter how full I come up, I am always sent back down empty. All that work, and I end exactly where I started."

The second bucket had heard this many times. "I have been thinking about the same rope," it said, "and I notice something different. No matter how empty I go down, I am always brought back up full."

"Those are the same thing," said the first bucket.

"They are," the second bucket agreed. "We do exactly the same work. But you spend the whole day dreading the trip down, and I spend the whole day expecting the trip up. At the end of it we have both carried the same water, and only one of us was miserable."

The first bucket said nothing for a while. Then it said, "That does not change the rope."

"No," said the second bucket. "It changes the day."

The well-keeper, who knew nothing of the conversation, worked until sundown and hung both buckets on their hooks. They had drawn the same amount of water. They had made the same number of trips. And each of them had lived a completely different day.

The lesson of this story is that two people can do identical work and have opposite experiences of it, because what a person expects at the start of a trip shapes what the trip feels like.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “The Two Buckets”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what traits, feelings, and motivations are shown through actions asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “The Two Buckets,” then answer: Trace how one example in the reading demonstrates traits, feelings, and motivations are shown through actions. Which step in the example does the most work?

Deliverable: Grade 3: a labeled explanation of the example and its most important step; write 3–5 complete sentences.

Evidence requirement: Use one exact detail. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If traits, feelings, and motivations are shown through actions is not yet secure, return to “The Two Buckets” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply traits, feelings, and motivations are shown through actions to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “The Two Buckets.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
